title: Token budgeting and dynamic batching labbook
body:
Purpose:
This labbook documents an exploratory sweep that connects token-budget strategies (max_tokens caps and per-request budgets), dynamic batching heuristics, and cache policies to observed latency/cost/quality tradeoffs for model-onboarding evals. The goals were: 1) produce reproducible latency & cost curves across workload slices, 2) identify robust default heuristics for Dedicated/Hosted routing, and 3) flag any quality regressions at aggressive budget points.

Background & motivation:
We onboarded a mid-size instruction-following open model (approx 6B params, GGML-like weights) to the runtime. Early runs showed strong P50 but poor P95 when small bursts hit the system; cost-per-token inflation at low batch sizes is suspected. Product asks for a pragmatic default that keeps latency SLOs while trimming token spend for typical web chat traffic (median input length ~22 tokens, high tail ~450 tokens).

Prompt set composition (for this sweep):
- 800 queries total, drawn from three buckets: short-ask (<=32 tokens) 60% (480), medium-context (33-128) 30% (240), long-context (>128) 10% (80).
- Labels: human rating set (200 samples priority), and automated metrics: embedding-sim (cosine vs baseline outputs), instruction-follow F1 on a small answer-key set (50 Q/A).
- Synthetic adversarial prompts (30) included to stress long-history KV cache behavior.

Experiment matrix (summary):
- max_tokens caps: [64, 128, 256, 512] applied per-request as a hard cutoff for generation.
- per-request token_budget (prompt + response cap): [input-preserve, 1.5x input, fixed 256] used in scheduled trimming logic.
- batching strategies: static batch sizes [1,4,8,16] and dynamic-batching heuristic that groups by current-queue-token-sum threshold (T=512 tokens) with max latency hold=25ms.
- cache policies: no-cache, prefix-cache (LRU keyed by first 64 tokens), kv-cache (full attention KV retained across rapid followups for same session id), and prefetch-lite (store last response embedding; quick mismatch fallback).
- routing: single-region (no cross-region fallback) to remove network variability.

Infrastructure & measurement notes:
- Runs executed on a Dedicated A100-ish pool with identical instance types.
- Each combo measured for 30k requests simulated with arrival process mimicking production burstiness (Poisson + occasional microbursts).
- Metrics captured: P50, P95, P99 latency (ms), tokens generated per request (avg), server-side CPU/GPU utilization, cost_estimated ($ per 1M tokens based on internal accounting), quality: embedding-sim mean, instruction-F1.
- All experiments seeded and logged to the evaluation bucket. Repro tags: sweep-aug25-2025-rt1.

Key results (high level):
1) Batching gains saturate quickly for short-medium prompts. Moving from batch=1 to batch=4 yields a 28% P50 token throughput gain for median queries; beyond batch=8 diminishing returns and P95 increases for synthetic microbursts.
2) The dynamic-batching heuristic (token-sum threshold T=512) provided the best balance: similar throughput to static batch=8 on heavy tails while keeping median latency near static=4. Dynamic-batching lowered average cost by ~9% vs conservative static=4 without measurable quality loss.
3) Max_tokens cap has nonlinear impact on quality/cost: capping at 64 cuts token spend by ~34% vs uncapped but reduces instruction-F1 by 0.12 absolute on the human sample (not acceptable for safety-critical flows). 256 is a reasonable inflection point for most web chat workloads (cost savings ~12%, F1 drop 0.03).
4) Cache policies: prefix-cache is low-cost and reduces repeated-token compute for short prompts with repeated prefixes (chat templates) by 15% tokens; kv-cache is the single biggest P95 improvement for in-session turn sequences (reduces P95 ~22%) but requires sticky session routing and increased memory. Prefetch-lite had low overhead but brittle on paraphrase-heavy traffic.

Representative numbers (median across runs):
- Baseline (no-cache, batch=1, uncapped): P50=140ms, P95=620ms, avg_tokens_gen=180, cost_est=$120 per 1M tokens, embedding-sim=0.86, F1=0.71.
- Dynamic-batching + kv-cache + max_tokens=256: P50=95ms, P95=420ms, avg_tokens_gen=160, cost_est=$106 per 1M tokens, embedding-sim=0.859, F1=0.69.
- Static batch=4 + prefix-cache + max_tokens=128: P50=105ms, P95=490ms, avg_tokens_gen=140, cost_est=$99 per 1M tokens, embedding-sim=0.854, F1=0.67.
- Aggressive cap max_tokens=64 + prefix-cache + static batch=8: P50=88ms, P95=730ms (microburst amplification), avg_tokens_gen=80, cost_est=$66 per 1M tokens, embedding-sim=0.82, F1=0.59 (human-rated quality drop notable).

Observations & interpretation:
- Tail latency (P95/P99) is sensitive to batching policy under bursty arrival; larger static batches amplify microburst tail due to queueing. Dynamic token-sum grouping reduces this by letting small short requests go through quickly even when the system backs up with long-context items.
- Cache choice depends on workload composition: sessions with multiple turns strongly benefit from kv-cache; one-off queries see limited benefit. Memory/eviction needs to be weighted against latency gains for Dedicated SKU sizing.
- Quality regressions begin to appear below ~128 token caps on this model for our instruction-follow tasks — careful gating required.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Need more controlled A/B with user-simulated session stickiness to validate kv-cache memory-pressure behavior (ticket: ENG-1327).
- Determine default token_budget strategy for Hosted tier: 1.5x input vs fixed upper-bound? Suggest running cost projections for both over a sampled production week.
- Explore adaptive max_tokens per-prompt using the prompt-classifier (small model predicts expected completion length) — quick prototype planned.

Operational recommendations (interim):
1) Adopt dynamic-batching (token-sum threshold T=512, max hold=25ms) as default for Hosted API for this model family; add telemetry flags to measure tail regressions.
2) Default max_tokens=256 for general Hosted; add opt-in lower caps for cost-conscious customers with documented quality tradeoffs.
3) Offer kv-cache as a Dedicated/Dedicated+ feature with guidance on session routing and memory sizing; default to prefix-cache for Hosted unless session affinity is enabled.
4) Add an onboarding checklist item: run the token-budget sweep (this matrix) and record P50/P95/cost_vs_quality curves into model-onboard metadata.

Appendix: brief run notes / quick failures:
- Run 7 (dynamic-batching + kv-cache) had an instrumentation bug (GPU-side token accounting double-counted 2% tokens) — excluded from final averages.
- Synthetic adversarial prompts revealed a cache poisoning-like pattern where near-duplicates with small edits caused cache misses and increased P95 — further TTL heuristics required.

Links & artifacts:
- Sweep logs and raw metrics: s3://redwood-eval/sweep-aug25-2025-rt1/ (internal).
- Related PR (runtime changes for dynamic-batching): https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487
- Linear ticket tracking followups: https://linear.app/RWINF/issue/ENG-1321-token-budgeting-sweep

Notes to self: keep the labbook raw and include more qualitative human-rating notes next pass; consider measuring per-token cost broken down by attention vs softmax kernel to inform quantization ROI.
